[THOUGHT]  
The patient presents with mucocutaneous bleeding (persistent post-extraction gingival bleeding, easy bruising) and a suggestive family history (uncle with bleeding, easy bruising, and joint swelling — classic for hemophilia A). Laboratory findings show:  
- Normal PT (15 sec → within typical reference range ~11–13.5 sec; though exact lab reference not provided, 15 sec is mildly elevated but not markedly so),  
- Prolonged aPTT (60 sec → significantly above normal, typically ~25–35 sec),  
- Severely low Factor VIII activity (12% of normal → consistent with moderate hemophilia A),  
- Normal vWF:Ag (95%) and vWF:RCo (93%), effectively ruling out von Willebrand disease,  
- Normal Factor IX (98%), excluding hemophilia B.  

The isolated low Factor VIII with normal vWF markers and prolonged aPTT strongly supports a diagnosis of **hemophilia A** (Factor VIII deficiency). The family history (X-linked recessive pattern — affected male relative) further corroborates this. No acquired causes (e.g., inhibitors, liver disease, medications) are present per history.

[SUMMARY]  
**Clinical Diagnosis:** Hemophilia A (moderate severity) — congenital Factor VIII deficiency.  

**Key Evidence:**  
- Clinical: Post-procedural mucosal bleeding, easy bruising, positive X-linked family history (affected maternal uncle with bleeding, bruising, and hemarthrosis).  
- Laboratory:  
  • aPTT markedly prolonged (60 sec); PT normal or near-normal → intrinsic pathway defect.  
  • Factor VIII activity: 12% of normal (normal: 50–150%; <5% = severe, 5–40% = moderate, >40% = mild).  
  • Normal vWF:Ag (95%) and vWF:RCo (93%) → excludes von Willebrand disease as cause of low FVIII.  
  • Normal Factor IX (98%) → excludes hemophilia B.  

**Next Steps Recommended:**  
- Confirm with inhibitor screen (Bethesda assay) to rule out acquired Factor VIII inhibitors (though unlikely given age, absence of prior factor exposure, and family history).  
- Genetic counseling and testing (F8 gene sequencing) for confirmation and carrier testing in female relatives.  
- Hematology referral for comprehensive management:  
  • On-demand or prophylactic Factor VIII concentrate replacement.  
  • Dental/surgical planning with hemostatic coverage.  
  • Patient education on bleeding recognition, avoidance of NSAIDs/antiplatelets, and emergency protocols.  
- Avoid intramuscular injections; use pressure, antifibrinolytics (e.g., tranexamic acid) adjunctively for mucosal bleeding.  

No evidence of liver disease, vitamin K deficiency, or medication-induced coagulopathy.

[THOUGHT]  
The case presents a classic, well-documented presentation of congenital hemophilia A (Factor VIII deficiency). The clinical phenotype — mucosal bleeding, easy bruising, hemarthrosis in a male relative, and X-linked inheritance pattern (affected maternal uncle) — strongly supports an X-linked recessive coagulopathy. Laboratory findings are diagnostic: markedly prolonged aPTT with normal PT localizes the defect to the intrinsic pathway; Factor VIII activity at 12% falls squarely within the moderate severity range (5–40%); preserved vWF antigen and ristocetin cofactor activity exclude von Willebrand disease as a cause of low FVIII; and normal Factor IX excludes hemophilia B. The absence of confounding conditions (e.g., liver disease, vitamin K deficiency, anticoagulant use) further strengthens the specificity of the diagnosis. While inhibitor screening is prudent before initiating replacement therapy, its absence does not undermine the diagnosis — inhibitors are rare de novo in untreated moderate hemophilia with strong family history, and the current lab and clinical data are fully concordant with congenital hemophilia A.

- Male patient with X-linked family history: affected maternal uncle with bleeding, bruising, and hemarthrosis.  
- Clinical phenotype includes post-procedural mucosal bleeding and easy bruising.  
- aPTT markedly prolonged (60 sec) with normal/near-normal PT → intrinsic pathway defect.  
- Factor VIII activity = 12% (within moderate hemophilia A range: 5–40%).  
- Normal vWF:Ag (95%) and vWF:RCo (93%) → rules out vWD-mediated FVIII reduction.  
- Normal Factor IX activity (98%) → excludes hemophilia B.  
- No evidence of liver disease, vitamin K deficiency, or medication-induced coagulopathy.

[GAPS]  
- Inhibitor screen (Bethesda assay) result is pending/not reported — critical before initiating factor replacement but not required to establish diagnosis.

[DIAGNOSIS]  
Hemophilia A (moderate severity)
